messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Carl is a 60-year-old warehouse worker who lives with his partner of thirty years in a small Midwestern town. He came to therapy at her urging, after months of escalating withdrawal and what she described as a “darkness” that had settled over him. The trauma that haunts Carl occurred during his military service, forty years ago, when he was a young soldier in a convoy ambushed in a narrow, dusty ravine. He remembers the heat, the smell of diesel and blood, and the moment the truck in front of him hit an IED. He watched his closest friend, a man named Reyes, die instantly, while Carl—shocked but physically unharmed—was pulled from the wreckage. For decades, he told himself it was just part of the job, something to bury and move past. But in the last few years, the memories have refused to stay buried.

When Carl tries to recall that day, he often finds himself stuck, unable to find the right words to describe what he saw or felt. He knows the facts, but the language to explain the terror and the guilt slips away, leaving him frustrated and mute. What does come back, unbidden and vivid, is the raw terror of the explosion—the same visceral fear he felt at that moment, as if he is back in the ravine. Worse than the fear is the guilt that surges with every memory. He has come to believe that he should have died instead of Reyes, that his survival was a mistake, a cosmic error. This belief has hollowed him out. He feels like he no longer knows who he is; the person he was before the ambush—a confident young man with a future—seems like a stranger. In its place is a hollow shell, certain that the world is fundamentally dangerous, that safety is an illusion. This conviction colors everything: a car backfiring on his street makes him drop to a crouch; a sudden loud noise in the warehouse sends his heart racing for hours.

Because he is certain the world is dangerous, Carl has developed a rigid set of strategies to keep himself safe. He avoids driving anywhere near the old military base on the outskirts of town, taking a twenty-minute detour that makes his commute absurdly long. At work, he refuses to wear the navy-blue coveralls required by the warehouse, because they remind him of the uniform he wore that day. He told his supervisor he had a skin allergy, and now he wears old, loose-fitting clothes that violate the dress code, earning him repeated warnings. More than anything, he avoids thinking about the event itself. When a memory starts to surface—triggered by a news report about a faraway war, or the sight of a dusty pickup truck that resembles a military vehicle—he forces his mind to go blank, distracting himself with menial tasks or counting objects on the shelves. This avoidance has become a full-time job. His partner has noticed that he no longer watches any movies with action or violence, and he has stopped visiting his brother, who lives near the base. The more he avoids, the more the world shrinks, and the more he feels he has lost his identity. He has begun to feel that his avoidance is proof that he is broken, that the real Carl—the one who could face life—is gone forever.

The memories themselves also drive his avoidance. When the terror of the ambush floods back, he feels an urgent need to escape his own mind. He will leave the dinner table mid-meal, or walk out of the grocery store, abandoning a full cart. He has learned that if he can just stop the memory from completing—by moving, by changing his environment—the guilt and fear will recede, at least temporarily. But the relief is short-lived. Each time he flees, his guilt deepens. He tells himself that he is a coward, that Reyes would have stayed and fought, that he does not deserve to be alive. This self-condemnation makes the next memory even more punishing, because it arrives already layered with shame. The cycle tightens: a memory triggers avoidance, avoidance confirms his guilt, and guilt makes the next memory more vivid and terrifying.

In the warehouse, the most difficult moments come when he has to unload a truck from a dusty loading dock. The smell of dry dirt and exhaust can send him reeling. He has started requesting the quietest, most isolated shifts—the overnight inventory count—where he can work alone, in silence, with minimal triggers. His supervisor has noticed his declining reliability and has written him up twice for leaving his station without explanation. Carl knows his job is at risk, but he cannot explain why he flees. What frightens him most is the growing sense that he is disappearing. He came to therapy because his partner told him she was afraid to come home to a man who sometimes seems not to be there at all. Carl is afraid of the same thing. He is terrified that if he lets himself remember fully, he will drown in the guilt. But he is equally terrified that the avoidance is erasing him, piece by piece.
